input:
The Antoine equation is a widely used empirical correlation that allows the vapour pressure of a pure substance to be estimated from its temperature, provided that a set of fitted constants is available for the substance in question. Here the substance is ethanol and the temperature of interest is 60 °C. The constants that go with the correlation are $A$ = 8.20417, $B$ = 1642.89 and $C$ = 230.3, with the pressure expressed in mmHg and the temperature in °C. In its usual form, the equation, which connects the vapour pressure, $P$, with the temperature, $T$, is written as
$$\log_{10} P = A - \frac{B}{T + C}$$
Carrying out the substitution with the values given above produces an estimate of 46.8 kPa for the vapour pressure. A number of qualifications nevertheless attach to this kind of estimate. The constants are valid only over their fitted temperature range, so the correlation should not be pushed beyond the range of the data from which it was derived. Furthermore, where a design figure is required, the source databank value governs design, and the Antoine estimate is best thought of as a convenient approximation that sits alongside the databank value rather than as a substitute for it. Taken together, these considerations mean that the estimate is a useful and readily obtained figure, as long as it is used within the bounds that its fitted constants impose. It is also helpful to remember that correlations of this kind earn their keep by being quick to evaluate and easy to embed in larger calculations, which is precisely why they remain in everyday use even though more fundamental treatments of vapour pressure exist.
target:
The vapour pressure of ethanol at 60 °C is estimated from the Antoine equation. The constants are $A$ = 8.20417, $B$ = 1642.89 and $C$ = 230.3, with pressure in mmHg and temperature in °C. The Antoine equation relates the vapour pressure, $P$, to the temperature, $T$, through the three fitted constants:
$$\log_{10} P = A - \frac{B}{T + C}$$
where $P$ denotes the vapour pressure and $T$ denotes the temperature. Substitution of the stated temperature gives an estimate of 46.8 kPa. The constants are empirical: they summarise measured vapour-pressure data over the temperature range to which they were fitted, and the relation is an interpolation device rather than a physical law. The form of the relation, a logarithm of pressure against a shifted reciprocal temperature, is chosen because vapour pressure rises steeply with temperature and the shift brings the curve close to a straight line over the fitted range. Each constant is tied to the units named with it, and the same numerical set cannot be carried into another unit system without refitting. The constants are valid only over their fitted temperature range. Outside that range the relation extrapolates a fitted curve beyond its evidence, and the error is not bounded by anything in the fit itself. The source databank value governs design, so the Antoine estimate serves as a check or a first value, and any design figure comes from the databank. The three constants belong to ethanol alone and to the stated unit system; another substance, or another set of units, requires its own fitted set. The estimate is therefore only as portable as its constants. At its stated scope, the result is an estimated vapour pressure at the stated temperature from the named constants, with the databank value standing as the governing figure wherever the two differ.
